And behold, today upon the throne of the house of Abbas the ruler is a Jew and the universal governor.
See how low pride has been brought down!
Yet from their wickedness and their insolence they do not desist or take heed.
And from here, complaints began to be heaped against Aruq,
among which a certain Persian scribe whose name was Abd al-Mu'min,
who also went to the camp and showed
that Aruq, his emirs, governors, and scribes had ruined all the countries and cities that were under Aruq's rule;
and that if they would strengthen his hand and support him,
he would extract one million gold dinars from them.
Now the emirs were pleased with such stories,
and they consented to the will of the slanderer,
though they held him back a little.
Now when Buqa saw that complaints against him and against his brother were being favorably received,
he took offense and withdrew backwards.
And he made himself sick,
and took to bed in his house.
And when the nobles came in to visit him, supposedly in his illness,
he would sigh before them and express regret for the good he had done for Arghun in the time of Ahmad,
and [said] that Arghun was not repaying him with reciprocal tokens of love.
And he began to contrive a secret plot of treachery and rebellion against Arghun,
and he revealed his secret to certain of the nobles.
And they in simplicity accepted this,
because they knew that he was a shrewd man,
and by his cunning Ahmad had been brought low,
and Arghun had triumphed.
Now Arghun, because he himself had personally experienced such a deed,
was guarding himself with vigilance.
The emirs, that is, those who were constantly in Arghun's service,
perceived the evil thought that had come to Buqa.
Now Buqa, when he realized that his treachery was exposed,
terror and fear and trembling fell upon him and he was bewildered,
and he did not know what to do.
He arose, mounted his horse,
and fled toward the camp of the Great Khatun Oljei {OCR?: Ilgei},
so that he might take refuge with her.
Arghun, however, and the rest of the emirs who were around him, as soon as they heard that Buqa had mounted [his horse],
mounted also themselves, pursued after him, and overtook him,
and they seized him and brought him [back].
And when they questioned him,
he confessed indeed:
"It was not the King of Kings that I wished to harm,
except those by deceit."
